title: Resilience After Losing a Spouse
text:
Most studies of grief begin after a death, which makes it hard to know how people were doing before. George Bonanno and his colleagues found a way around this. A large study called Changing Lives of Older Couples had interviewed about 1,500 married people aged 65 and over in the Detroit area. Over the following years, some of them lost their husband or wife.

Bonanno's team examined about 200 of these widowed people, comparing their depression and well-being before the loss with measures taken six and eighteen months after it. That allowed them to trace distinct paths through bereavement.

The most common path, followed by close to half, was resilience. These people felt sadness and longing, but their depression stayed low throughout, and they continued functioning in their daily lives. Smaller groups showed what had long been assumed to be the usual pattern, grief that rose and then eased, or chronic grief that persisted. Another group had been depressed before the loss and remained so, and some who had been depressed in unhappy marriages actually improved after the spouse died.

Resilient widows and widowers were not cold or detached. They had generally had good marriages and missed their spouses. The study challenged the belief that the absence of intense distress means something is wrong.
lesson: There is no single right way to grieve. Steady functioning after a loss is common and healthy, not a sign of denial or lack of love.
people: George Bonanno, Camille Wortman, Darrin Lehman and colleagues
source: Bonanno, G. A., Wortman, C. B., Lehman, D. R., Tweed, R. G., Haring, M., Sonnega, J., Carr, D., and Nesse, R. M. (2002). Resilience to loss and chronic grief: A prospective study from preloss to 18-months postwidowhood. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1150-1164.
